content.text: The text discusses chronic tubercular and cancerous peritonitis, emphasizing diagnostic difficulty, physical examination, pulmonary signs, ascitic-fluid characteristics, pathology, prognosis, and largely palliative treatment. Tubercular disease commonly produces fever, meteorism, longer duration, and pulmonary involvement; cancerous peritonitis produces syrupy, albumin-rich fluid, nodules, obstruction, and relatively little fever. A detailed case describes a woman who became ill at her family’s country home, was later brought to her city home, repeatedly tapped for ascites, and ultimately died from intestinal obstruction due to ovarian scirrhous carcinoma. The text then covers infantile peritonitis, ascites and its causes, examination, and treatment. Finally, it introduces tabes mesenterica—tuberculosis of mesenteric glands—describing its causes, pathology, symptoms in children, diagnosis, unfavorable prognosis, prevention, nutritional support, and palliation.
